extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate or beginning graduate students in topology/real analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and states key necessary/sufficient conditions and constructions about quotient spaces, separation axioms, Urysohn’s Lemma, metrization, Ascoli–Arzelà, and Stone–Weierstrass from a topology/analysis textbook chapter. Focus is on hypotheses → conclusions for these standard theorems and corollaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: quotient topology / quotient map
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an equivalence relation ~ on X and the projection q : X → X/~, a subset U of X/~ is defined to be open in the quotient topology iff q^{-1}(U) is open in X. The projection q is called the quotient map.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard definition used throughout; many subsequent propositions assert properties of maps factoring through the quotient or when the quotient inherits separation/compactness properties. Use this definition when checking openness of sets in a quotient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: open map
rubrics_metrics.description: A function F : X → Y between topological spaces is open if F carries open sets to open sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in corollaries (e.g., if F is continuous, onto, and open then Y is a quotient and resulting map is a homeomorphism). Check openness of coordinate projections in product spaces as examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 10.38 (Universal mapping property for quotients)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If F : X → Y is continuous and constant on each equivalence class of an equivalence relation ~ on X (i.e., x1 ~ x2 ⇒ F(x1)=F(x2)), then there exists a well-defined continuous f : X/~ → Y with F = f ◦ q. (b) Conversely, the quotient X/~ is characterized by this universal property: any continuous surjection q' : X → Z that is constant on equivalence classes and satisfies the analogous universality is canonically homeomorphic to X/~.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives the criterion for when a function factors through the quotient and provides a means to recognize a space as a quotient: check that the map is continuous, surjective, and constant on equivalence classes (and satisfies the universality condition). The proof reduces continuity questions to preimages via q.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 10.39 (Quotient by an open continuous surjection yields homeomorphism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let F : X → Y be a continuous surjection and q : X → X/~ the quotient map induced by the equivalence x1 ~ x2 iff F(x1)=F(x2). If F is open (in addition to continuous and onto), then the induced map f : X/~ → Y is a homeomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove f is a homeomorphism, show it is continuous, bijective, and open (openness of F and properties of q are used). Example: coordinate projections p_s from a product are open, so factors are quotients via the described relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: coordinate projection is open
rubrics_metrics.description: For the product X = ∏_s X_s and fixed s, the projection p_s : X → X_s is an open map: basic open sets map to open sets in X_s, hence p_s is open and X_s can be regarded as the quotient of X by the relation x1 ~ x2 iff p_s(x1)=p_s(x2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a standard example to verify openness of projections and recognize factor spaces as quotients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 10.40 (Hausdorff quotient criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X be a topological space and ~ an equivalence relation on X. Let R = { (x1,x2) ∈ X×X : x1 ~ x2 }. If the quotient X/~ is Hausdorff, then R is a closed subset of X×X. Conversely, if R is closed in X×X and the quotient map q : X → X/~ is open, then X/~ is Hausdorff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a necessary condition (Hausdorff quotient ⇒ equivalence relation is closed) and a sufficient condition (closed relation + open quotient map ⇒ Hausdorff). Use product topology arguments and separation of q(x), q(y) by disjoint open sets to prove these implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 10.41 (Quotient by closure-equivalence in regular spaces)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a regular topological space X define x ~ y iff x ∈ cl{y} and y ∈ cl{x} (equivalence via closures). Let q : X → X/~ be the quotient map. Then (a) q is open and every open set in X is a union of equivalence classes; (b) X/~ is regular and Hausdorff; (c) X normal implies X/~ normal; (d) X separable implies X/~ separable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that passing to the closure-equivalence quotient improves separation (gives Hausdorff) and preserves many desirable properties. To check Hausdorff, apply Proposition 10.40 and show R is closed using regularity; openness of q follows because opens are unions of classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 10.42 (Urysohn’s Lemma)
rubrics_metrics.description: If E and F are disjoint closed sets in a normal topological space X, then there exists a continuous function f : X → [0,1] with f = 0 on E and f = 1 on F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct nested open sets around E and away from F indexed by dyadic rationals and define f(x) as the infimum of dyadic r with x ∈ U_r. This is the standard Urysohn construction; it is used to separate closed sets by continuous functions and underpins many later results (e.g., Tietze extension, metrization arguments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 10.43 (Urysohn for compact Hausdorff)
rubrics_metrics.description: If E and F are disjoint closed sets in a compact Hausdorff space X, then there exists a continuous f : X → [0,1] that is 0 on E and 1 on F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combines compactness + Hausdorff to obtain normality, then apply Urysohn’s Lemma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 10.44 (Urysohn with compact support in locally compact Hausdorff)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is locally compact Hausdorff, K ⊆ X compact, F closed and disjoint from K, then there exists a continuous f : X → [0,1] that is 1 on K, 0 on F, and has compact support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses one-point compactification X* to reduce to compact Hausdorff case, applies Urysohn there, and restricts back to X to obtain a function with compact support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 10.45 (Urysohn Metrization Theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any separable regular Hausdorff space X is homeomorphic to a subspace of the Hilbert cube [0,1]^∞ and hence is metrizable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take a countable base B and for each pair (U,V) of base elements with closure(U) ⊆ V use Urysohn’s Lemma to get continuous functions f_n separating them; embed X via F(x) = (f_n(x)) into the Hilbert cube. Show F is continuous, injective, and has open image in its subspace topology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 10.46 (Separable compact Hausdorff metrizable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every separable compact Hausdorff space is metrizable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate from compactness + Theorem 10.45 (compact ⇒ separable regular Hausdorff) and embedding in Hilbert cube.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: equicontinuity and pointwise boundedness
rubrics_metrics.description: A family F of scalar-valued functions on X is equicontinuous at x if for each ε>0 there exists a neighborhood U_x,ε of x such that |f(y)-f(x)| < ε for all y ∈ U_x,ε and all f ∈ F. F is equicontinuous if equicontinuous at each x. F is pointwise bounded if for each x the set { |f(x)| : f ∈ F } is bounded; uniformly bounded if sup_{f∈F} sup_{x∈X} |f(x)| < ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These notions replace uniform equicontinuity in nonmetric settings; equicontinuity is essential hypothesis in Ascoli–Arzelà-type compactness results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 10.47 (Closure of equicontinuous family is equicontinuous)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F is equicontinuous at x ∈ X, then the closure cl(F) in the product topology on C(X) is also equicontinuous at x. Consequently every member of cl(F) is continuous at x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof uses closedness of sets defined by uniform small oscillation on some neighborhood and takes intersections over ε>0. Use to pass equicontinuity to limits in product topology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 10.48 (Ascoli–Arzelà Theorem, extended)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X be compact Hausdorff. If a sequence {f_n} of scalar-valued functions on X is pointwise bounded (bounded at each x) and equicontinuous, then {f_n} has a uniformly convergent subsequence (i.e., a subsequence converging in C(X) uniformly). Equivalently, an equicontinuous pointwise-bounded family has relatively compact closure in the product/C(X) topology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Tychonoff compactness of ∏_x closed bounded intervals to obtain a limit point in product topology, Lemma 10.47 to get equicontinuity, and a diagonal/finite-subcover argument to obtain uniform convergence. This is the generalization of the metric Ascoli theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 10.49 (Characterization of compact subsets of C(X))
rubrics_metrics.description: For X compact Hausdorff, a subset F ⊆ C(X) is compact iff (a) F is closed in C(X), (b) F is equicontinuous, and (c) F is pointwise bounded (hence uniformly bounded).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Necessity: compact ⇒ closed and bounded; equicontinuity is deduced from total boundedness arguments. Sufficiency: use Ascoli (every sequence has uniformly convergent subsequence) plus completeness of C(X) to get compactness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 10.50 (Stone–Weierstrass Theorem, extended)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If A is a real subalgebra of C(X; R) that separates points and contains the constants, then A is dense in C(X; R) in the uniform norm. (b) If A is a complex subalgebra of C(X; C) that separates points, contains constants, and is closed under complex conjugation, then A is dense in C(X; C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard extension of Stone–Weierstrass to compact Hausdorff spaces. Remarks note that Urysohn’s Lemma is not used in the proof (the proof mirrors the metric case); the theorem supplies dense algebras of continuous functions used in approximation theory and functional analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applications/examples and problem-guided criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous problems and examples apply the above results: e.g., constructing non-normal Hausdorff regular spaces using Urysohn’s Lemma for contradiction; recognizing quotient spaces homeomorphic to familiar spaces (circle as quotient of interval), characterizing order topologies, and producing partitions of unity and Tietze extension via Urysohn constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems list concrete criteria and constructions students should be able to verify: checking closedness of relation subsets to determine Hausdorffness of quotients; building continuous functions separating sets; constructing embeddings into product spaces; producing locally finite covers and partitions of unity in normal spaces; iterating Urysohn constructions to obtain Tietze extensions.
